name: Benzphetamine

lead: Benzphetamine (Didrex) is an older prescription appetite suppressant related to amphetamine. It reduces hunger so people eat less and lose weight, working toward a leaner look.

It is thought to increase norepinephrine and dopamine release in the brain's feeding centers, and the body converts it to amphetamine and methamphetamine. In the US it is labelled as a short-term add-on, lasting a few weeks, to a reduced-calorie diet for people with a BMI of 30 or higher.

paras: It is taken as a pill under prescription for a short period alongside a calorie-restricted diet. The label states it is not for long-term use.

Reported effects include raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia and restlessness. The label cites an association between long-term anorectic use and pulmonary hypertension and contraindicates use in pregnancy. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US.

angle.text: Benzphetamine is a stimulant appetite suppressant that lowers calorie intake and leads to weight loss and a leaner look. It is a prescription obesity medication labelled for a few weeks of use.

lead: Benzphetamine (brand name Didrex, among others) is a prescription sympathomimetic amine used as an appetite suppressant. In the United States it is labelled as a short-term adjunct, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted weight-reduction regimen for people with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet and exercise alone. [1][2][3]
It is related to amphetamines and is described as a prodrug that the body converts to amphetamine and methamphetamine. [3][1] It is a controlled substance, listed in Schedule III in the US. [3][1]

Its relevance to appearance culture is as one of the older prescription anorectics used for fat loss. The US label states the drug is not for long-term use, and no published community material about it is catalogued here.
infobox: Schedule III controlled substance, prescription only [3]

paras: The US label indicates benzphetamine for the management of exogenous obesity as a short-term adjunct to caloric restriction in patients with a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet or exercise alone. [2] Grokipedia states the drug was approved in 1960 and that clinical trials showed modest additional weight loss over placebo that plateaued after the early weeks, with tolerance developing. [1] These trial figures come from an AI-generated source and were not verified against primary trial reports.

The label lists palpitations, tachycardia and elevated blood pressure among cardiovascular effects, along with central nervous system effects such as overstimulation, restlessness and insomnia. [2] It warns against combining benzphetamine with other anorectic agents. [2]

The label notes a case-control study in which anorectic drugs used for longer than three months were associated with a 23-fold increase in the risk of pulmonary hypertension, a rare and often fatal condition. [2] Valvular heart disease has been reported with some anorectics such as fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine; the label says no such cases had been reported with benzphetamine. [2] The drug is contraindicated in pregnancy. [2] Listed contraindications include advanced arteriosclerosis, symptomatic cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, agitation, a history of drug misuse and recent monoamine oxidase inhibitor use. [3][1]

Benzphetamine is thought to act like other amphetamines by promoting release of norepinephrine and dopamine in the hypothalamic feeding center, reducing appetite; Wikipedia notes its exact mechanism is not fully established. [3] Tachyphylaxis and tolerance to appetite-suppressing effects are described for the class. [3] Wikipedia gives its elimination half-life as 4 to 6 hours, while Grokipedia gives 16 to 31 hours, so published figures differ. [3][1] Plasma protein binding is listed as 75 to 99%. [3]

Benzphetamine is scheduled differently across countries: Schedule III in the US, Schedule I in Canada, Class C in the UK, prescription-only (S4) in Australia, and restricted to authorised scientific use in Germany. [3] Wikipedia describes the US Schedule III listing as unusual for an amphetamine-related drug. [3] It is the parent compound of the related anorectic clobenzorex. [3]
